chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub narrated from a number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from Abdullah ibn Yahya, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a Mutamatti' (one who performs Hajj al-Tamattu') who fasted three days during Hajj, then offered a sacrificial animal (Hady) on the day he left Mina. He said, 'His fasting suffices for him.'

key_terms.أَجْزَأَهُ: It suffices for him / It is accepted as sufficient fulfillment.
key_terms.ثَلَاثَةَ أَيَّامٍ: Three days, referring to the days of Tashriq or specific days of fasting for the Tamattu' pilgrim.
key_terms.مُتَمَتِّعٍ: A pilgrim who performs Umrah first, then Hajj, in the same season.
key_terms.هَدْيًا: A sacrificial animal (sheep, goat, cow, or camel) offered by the pilgrim.
key_terms.يَوْمَ خَرَجَ مِنْ مِنًى: The day of leaving Mina, typically the 12th or 13th of Dhu al-Hijjah.

ai.seo_question: Does a Mutamatti' pilgrim need to offer a sacrificial animal if they have already fasted three days during Hajj?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that for a Mutamatti' pilgrim, the mandatory three-day fast suffices as the complete fulfillment of the Hady obligation, rendering the actual slaughter of an animal unnecessary in this specific scenario. This ruling highlights the flexibility within Shia fiqh regarding the modes of expiation (Kaffarah) for Hajj, emphasizing that the spiritual discipline of fasting can serve as a valid and sufficient substitute for the physical act of sacrifice when conditions are met. The hadith underscores the principle that the intent and performance of the prescribed act (fasting) are paramount, allowing pilgrims ease during the Hajj season.
